newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: High voter turnout in cliffhanger NZ election.
newsitem.headline: High voter turnout in cliffhanger NZ election.

text.p: New Zealand voters rushed to polls in huge numbers on Saturday in what was forecast to be a knife-edge contest in the first election under a new proportional system.

Chief electoral officer Phil Whelan said the turnout looked set to be the highest ever. Queues began forming half an hour before polling booths opened in the morning, and by 3.00 p.m. (0200 GMT) turnout had not abated.

"I haven't spoken to all the returning officers... but those that we have spoken to have indicated right across the board that it is a very high turnout with queues in some places," Whelan told Radio New Zealand.
Deputy Chief Electoral Officer Hugh Garland doubted many voters would be deterred by deteriorating weather. "It's an historic occasion. People will want to be involved."
Of 2.4 million eligible voters, 92 percent had registered when electoral rolls closed on Friday.
Voters have a choice of 21 parties ranging from the Natural Law Party advocating yogic flying to the pro-marijuna Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis Party and the McGillicuddy Serious Party.
Pre-election polls suggest an extremely close contest between the ruling conservative National Party and the centre-left Labour Party, backed by the more left-wing Alliance Party.
The major concern expressed at this stage is that some parties are breaking the rules for election day. There were complaints from voters in some cities that political posters had not been removed.
Political advertising is banned on election day. Whelan said parties which still had hoardings in place had been asked to take them down.
Polls close at 7.00 p.m. (0600 GMT) and counting is expected to be completed four hours later.
Unlike under the former first-past-the-post system, a clear decision on who rules may not be known for weeks. A government will only be agreed after complex negotiations.

The last pre-election poll suggested National with its probable allies -- the radical free-market Act New Zealand and the centrist United Party -- would have 50 seats in the expanded 120 seat parliament.
That number would be precisely matched by Labour and the Alliance, leaving New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, a charismatic Maori, as kingmaker with his party's 20 seats.
Peters has hinted his party would back Labour leader Helen Clark in her bid to be the country's first woman prime minister.
But he has kept his options open, campaigning for more open and accountable government and limits on foreign ownership, particularly of "strategic" assets.
Issues came second to coalition bargaining during the lacklustre five-week campaign.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger said the election was a choice between the stable orthodox economic policies of the past six years, which have brought growth and jobs, and leftist plans to roll back free market reforms.

Clark, seen by commentators to have run a flawless campaign hugely increasing her personal and party's standing, said the election was about spreading the fruits of New Zealand's economic recovery more evenly.
She has promised to spend more on education and health, paid for by higher taxes on the wealthy.

Bolger saw a 20-point lead over Labour earlier this year shrink to four points by this week. He attempted to rally flagging support by suggesting Labour was teaming up with "old fashioned socialists".
